strengths: Extremely thorough, systematic ablation study of CLIP training design choices specifically for the 3D medical imaging domain (report length/augmentation, field-of-view vs patch size trade-offs, token aggregation, batch size/loss variants), providing genuinely useful best-practice guidance that is currently missing from the literature.

Novel combination, in the 3D medical domain, of contrastive language-image pretraining, a CapPa-style report-generation objective, and MAE-based vision-only self-supervision to leverage both paired and unpaired data — no prior 3D medical VLE work has combined all three.

Strong and consistent empirical gains: the resulting COLIPRI encoders achieve state-of-the-art classification probing, competitive/near-SOTA zero-shot classification versus fVLM (without needing organ segmentation masks), and substantial improvements in clinically-relevant report generation metrics (RadBERT, RadFact) over CT-CLIP, CT-FM, and Merlin.

Broad, holistic evaluation spanning retrieval, linear probing, zero-shot classification (with two complementary prompting protocols), report generation (lexical and clinical metrics), and downstream segmentation — going beyond a single-task validation.
Good transparency and reproducibility: detailed appendix on preprocessing, prompts used for LLM-based report restructuring/shortening, evaluation protocols, and metric definitions.

Identification of an important and underappreciated failure mode — sensitivity of zero-shot classification to prompt style (native long-form vs short-form) — which is a valuable diagnostic contribution for the community beyond the main method.

Honest, non-cherry-picked discussion of limitations, including that the combined objectives do not improve (and can slightly hurt) linear probing/zero-shot metrics relative to CLIP-only, and that segmentation benefits are minimal, with plausible explanations offered (regularization effects, low-level voxel reconstruction vs semantic alignment mismatch).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an adaptation/combination of existing 2D techniques (CapPa, MAE, SigLIP2-style alternation of objectives) to a new domain rather than a fundamentally new method; novelty is primarily empirical/engineering rather than conceptual.

The 'comprehensive' final model (COLIPRI-CRM) does not clearly dominate — individual variants (COLIPRI-C, -CR, -CM) are often best on specific metrics/tasks, undermining the central claim that combining all three objectives yields the best overall encoder; this inconsistency is not fully resolved or explained beyond post-hoc hypotheses.

Segmentation results, the paper's main testbed for 'dense task' benefit, show only marginal or no improvement over training from scratch and clearly underperform a simple MAE baseline, weakening the argument that the added vision-only objective meaningfully improves dense representations.

All experiments are restricted to chest CT with one vision backbone (Primus-M) and one text encoder (CXR-BERT); generalization to other anatomies, modalities (MRI), or architectures is untested, limiting claims of broad applicability implied by 'comprehensive'.

Absolute performance on clinically meaningful report-generation metrics remains low (RadFact-CT F1(+) ~20, RadBERT MacroF1 ~40), and no human/radiologist evaluation is provided to validate that gains translate to clinical usefulness.

Extensive hyperparameter sweeps and design choices are tuned on a fairly small internal validation split (1k CT-RATE subjects) reused repeatedly across many sequential ablations, raising some risk of overfitting to this specific validation set even though a held-out test set is used for final reporting.

Zero-shot classification remains highly prompt-sensitive (up to ~7-10 AUROC/AUPRC point gap between 'native' and 'short' prompting), which is acknowledged but not solved, limiting practical zero-shot usability despite being framed as a key capability of the approach.

Baseline comparisons partly rely on numbers reported in other papers (e.g., fVLM, BIUD) with excluded classes or under different evaluation protocols, and CT-CLIP's discrepant reproduced performance versus literature values is only briefly noted as a possible 'configuration issue' without full resolution.

strengths: Extensive and systematic ablation studies covering report-length effects, field-of-view/patch-size/token-aggregation choices, batch-size/loss-type trade-offs, and hyperparameters for both the RRG and MAE objectives, providing a useful set of empirically-grounded design recommendations for 3D medical CLIP training.

Reasonably novel combination for the 3D medical domain: pairing a contrastive objective with a CapPa-style report-generation objective and an MAE-style vision-only objective to exploit both paired and unpaired CT data, which the paper credibly argues has not been previously explored together in 3D medical imaging.

Strong, broad experimental evaluation spanning classification probing, zero-shot classification, report generation (lexical and clinical metrics), and semantic segmentation, with comparisons against multiple relevant baselines (CT-CLIP, CT-FM, Merlin, fVLM, BIUD).

Good transparency about limitations: the paper explicitly reports sensitivity to prompt formulation in zero-shot classification, the lack of segmentation gains from the added objectives, and discrepancies with baseline numbers reported in prior work.
High reproducibility effort: detailed preprocessing pipelines, LLM prompts for report restructuring/shortening, and hyperparameter settings are provided in the appendix.
Qualitative PCA visualizations provide an intuitive illustration of the improved spatial coherence of the learned dense features relative to baselines.
weaknesses: The central 'comprehensive' framing is undercut by the actual results: combining the CLIP, RRG, and MAE objectives (COLIPRI-CRM) frequently underperforms simpler variants (e.g., COLIPRI-C) on classification probing and native zero-shot metrics, suggesting the objectives do not synergize as claimed and the paper does not fully resolve why, beyond post-hoc 'regularization' hypotheses.

The 'native' zero-shot classification protocol, which averages embeddings from 50 labeled positive and 50 labeled negative reports per abnormality, is not zero-shot in the standard CLIP sense (a single text prompt); it is closer to a prototype/few-shot classifier built from labeled examples, yet it is presented alongside true zero-shot ('short') results as if directly comparable, which risks overstating the model's zero-shot capability.

Segmentation results show essentially no benefit (and sometimes a deficit) from the proposed vision-language pretraining relative to a plain MAE baseline, undermining the claim of producing broadly 'comprehensive' general-purpose embeddings suited to dense downstream tasks.

All pretraining, ablation, and most evaluation is restricted to chest CT (CT-RATE/NLST/RAD-ChestCT); no experiments demonstrate generalization to other anatomical regions or modalities, limiting evidence for broader applicability of the proposed best practices.

Baseline comparisons have some fairness concerns acknowledged by the authors themselves (e.g., CT-CLIP reproducing much lower than published numbers, fVLM comparisons excluding two abnormality classes), which weakens confidence in the magnitude of reported improvements.

Absolute performance on report generation remains low in clinical terms (RadBERT MacroF1 ~40, RadFact-CT F1(+) ~20), and while this is disclosed, it tempers the practical significance of the reported gains over baselines.

Extensive hyperparameter search (star sweeps) is conducted using only a single held-out CT-RATE validation split, raising some risk that design choices are overfit to this particular dataset's characteristics rather than reflecting generally optimal practices.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-engineered combination of contrastive vision-language alignment, radiology report generation (RRG), masked autoencoding (MAE), and a novel Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) into a unified 3D VLE framework, with each component's contribution carefully isolated via staged ablations (COLIPRI-C/CR/CM/CRM).

Extensive and systematic hyperparameter/ablation studies (report length handling, FOV/patch size, batch size, loss type, augmentation strength, text encoder choice, MAE masking strategy, etc.) that establish useful best practices for the underexplored 3D medical vision-language domain.

The proposed OSL directly and convincingly addresses a well-motivated practical problem -- the mismatch between long-form training reports and short zero-shot query phrasing -- with clear ablation evidence (Tab. 3, Tab. B.1) showing it closes most of the gap between native and short-prompt zero-shot performance.

Strong, broad empirical evaluation spanning zero-shot classification, linear probing, retrieval, report generation, and segmentation across two datasets (CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT) and multiple established baselines (CT-CLIP, Merlin, CT-FM, fVLM, BIUD, 2D models), with consistent state-of-the-art results and reported confidence intervals/bootstrap statistics.

Thoughtful use of both paired (CT-RATE) and unpaired (NLST) data via alternating vision-only/vision-language objectives to increase effective training data, addressing a genuine data scarcity bottleneck in 3D medical VLP.

Honest and specific limitations discussion (e.g., RRG objective yields only marginal gains, absolute clinical metrics remain below clinical-utility thresholds, transformer encoders still lag CNNs on segmentation), which strengthens rather than undermines the paper's credibility.
Detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, prompts, preprocessing pipeline) provided in supplementary material, and code/model release is promised.
weaknesses: The work is restricted entirely to chest CT (single anatomical region and modality); despite the 'comprehensive' framing, generalization to other body regions, modalities (MRI), or institutions is untested, limiting the claimed breadth of contribution.

The training-data preprocessing pipeline depends heavily on a proprietary LLM (GPT-4o) for translation, restructuring into clinical subsections, and sentence shortening/labeling; this is a black-box, non-reproducible, and potentially costly component that is also central to enabling the OSL and RRG objectives, and no error analysis of this LLM-based preprocessing is given.

Evaluation uses RadFact, which itself is computed via GPT-4o judgments; combined with GPT-4o-based training data curation, this raises some concern about evaluation independence/circularity, though the metric itself is externally established.

The CT-CLIP baseline reproduced by the authors underperforms substantially relative to numbers reported in the original CT-CLIP/fVLM papers, attributed only vaguely to unspecified 'configuration issues', which weakens confidence in some baseline comparisons even though both sets of numbers are reported for transparency.

Despite state-of-the-art relative gains, absolute clinical performance for report generation remains low (RadBERT MacroF1 ~45%, RadFact-CT(+) F1 ~22%), and the paper acknowledges the model is not yet clinically usable, tempering the practical significance of the reported improvements.

Individual technical components (CapPa-style captioning, MAE, CLIP, sigmoid vs. softmax loss comparisons) are largely adapted from existing general-domain techniques rather than newly proposed; novelty is concentrated mainly in the OSL and the specific combination/engineering choices for the 3D medical setting.

The RRG objective, a headline contribution, is shown to have minimal impact on final report-generation quality and mixed effects on other tasks, suggesting the objective formulation is not yet well-optimized, which is acknowledged but not resolved.

Comparisons to fVLM for zero-shot classification are somewhat confounded since fVLM relies on segmentation masks at inference time while COLIPRI does not use masks; although this is noted by the authors, it complicates direct performance interpretation.

strengths: Comprehensive, multi-faceted evaluation spanning classification probing, zero-shot classification, retrieval, report generation, and semantic segmentation, with consistent SOTA or near-SOTA results against strong baselines (CT-CLIP, Merlin, CT-FM, fVLM, BIUD, 2D VLEs).

The Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) is a genuinely novel and well-motivated contribution that directly addresses the train/inference linguistic distribution shift (long reports vs. short zero-shot prompts), and ablations (Tab. 3) convincingly show its benefit.

Very thorough and transparent ablation studies (hundreds of configurations across FOV/patch size, token pooling, text augmentation, RRG decoding mode, MAE masking strategy, batch size, etc.) that constitute a useful 'best practices' resource for the 3D medical VLE community, going beyond a single-method paper.

Careful combination of vision-only (MAE) and vision-language objectives to leverage both paired and unpaired 3D CT data, with clear empirical demonstration (Tab. D.5) that this materially improves dense-task performance without excessively harming global alignment.
High reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, LLM prompts for report restructuring, dataset preprocessing pipeline, and stated intent to release code/weights.

Honest, substantive limitations discussion (RRG's marginal benefit, gap between probing and zero-shot, transformer vs CNN segmentation gap, clinically low absolute report-generation accuracy) rather than perfunctory boilerplate.
Qualitative PCA visualizations (Fig. 1) provide compelling, interpretable evidence of improved dense feature quality relative to baselines.
weaknesses: All pre-training and evaluation is confined to chest CT (CT-RATE + NLST, with RAD-ChestCT only for classification); it is unclear how well the approach and its design choices (e.g., FOV/patch-size findings) generalize to other anatomies or modalities (MRI, abdominal/whole-body CT).

The overall system is largely a careful engineering combination of existing techniques (CLIP, CapPa-style parallel captioning, MAE, attention pooling) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the paper's main novel algorithmic contribution is essentially the OSL, with the rest being adaptation/best-practices work (which is a valid contribution type but should be judged accordingly).

The RRG objective's isolated benefit is small and sometimes counter to the paper's own hypothesis (Sec. 5.3 notes minimal RRG contribution to report generation despite being explicitly designed for it), raising questions about whether this component is well understood or necessary in the final recipe.
Absolute clinical performance for report generation remains low (RadBERT Macro-F1 ~45%, RadFact-CT(+) F1 ~22%), which the authors acknowledge, but this tempers claims of clinical readiness/impact.

Heavy reliance on an LLM (GPT-4o) for translation, restructuring, and sentence categorization of reports, with no human/expert validation of the quality or potential bias/hallucination introduced by this automated preprocessing pipeline.

Discrepancies between the authors' reproduced CT-CLIP results and originally reported values (attributed to unspecified 'configuration issues') raise minor concerns about the fairness/reliability of baseline comparisons, even though both sets of numbers are reported transparently.

Transformer-based Primus-M encoder still underperforms CNN (ResEnc-L) baselines on segmentation, indicating that the architectural backbone itself remains a limiting factor not fully resolved by the proposed pre-training objectives.

No external, held-out multi-institutional test set is used; nearly all quantitative evaluation derives from splits of the same CT-RATE source data (aside from RAD-ChestCT classification), limiting evidence of broader generalization.
